extracted.intended_audience: immigration practitioners, affected aliens and sponsors, USCIS/DOJ officials, and public commenters on the proposed rule
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory preamble and proposed regulatory text describing DHS/USCIS policies, procedures, and standards for permitting, setting, maintaining, substituting, breaching, and cancelling public charge bonds in the adjustment-of-status context.

rubrics_metrics.name: USCIS discretion to permit posting a public charge bond
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitting an alien found inadmissible as a public charge (but otherwise admissible) to submit a public charge bond is within DHS’s discretion under section 213 of the Act; USCIS will notify the alien of the possibility to submit a bond when a favorable exercise of discretion is warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS will specify the bond amount and conditions and the alien may submit the appropriate form and fee only after USCIS makes the option available; unsolicited bond submissions will be rejected. The same factors that weighed in the public-charge inadmissibility determination generally inform whether offering a bond is warranted, though DHS may consider a range of positive and negative discretionary factors (e.g., national security benefits, exceptional humanitarian reasons, family unity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship to Affidavit of Support (distinct but complementary)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Affidavit of Support (Form I-864) is a separate, enforceable contract between a sponsor and the U.S. Government; the public charge bond is a distinct contractual mechanism between the United States and an obligor to guarantee certain conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bonds are to be considered in addition to, not instead of, affidavit-of-support and deeming requirements under section 213A. Unlike an affidavit of support (where the sponsored alien and various agencies may enforce obligations), only the government (obligee) may pursue recovery under the bond and only the obligor may challenge a breach determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum bond amount (base and annual adjustment)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes a new minimum public charge bond amount of $10,000, adjusted annually for inflation (CPI-U) and rounded up to the nearest dollar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The $10,000 base replaces the historical statutory reference to $1,000 (1964 dollars). USCIS will consider the alien’s individual circumstances when determining the exact bond amount in a given case. DHS solicits comment on whether the minimum should be higher or lower and possible ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond amount non-appealable
rubrics_metrics.description: If USCIS determines the alien may submit a public charge bond, neither the alien nor obligor (including a surety) may administratively appeal the amount required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS relies on the discretionary nature of section 213 authority and concludes that neither the AAO nor the BIA has jurisdiction to review this discretionary determination. The bond amount is set “in such amount and containing such conditions” as DHS prescribes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of bonds accepted and initial operational limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule retains options for surety bonds or cash/cash-equivalent bonds (e.g., cashier’s check, money order, deposit and agreement), but USCIS plans initially to accept only surety bonds for operational feasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surety bonds avoid the immediate exchange of cash and related accounting/interest management. USCIS will use a new Form I-945, Public Charge Bond, and proposes a $25 processing fee submitted with Form I-945.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable surety companies standard
rubrics_metrics.description: For public charge surety bonds, an acceptable surety generally must appear on the current Treasury Department Circular 570 as certified to underwrite Federal bonds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treasury-certified sureties have been evaluated for corporate and financial standards and hold the requisite certificate of authority. Under 31 U.S.C. 9305(b)(3) sureties (and obligors) must carry out contracts and promptly pay demands arising from administratively final breach determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond submission procedure and form/fee compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: A public charge bond submission must be on the form designated (Form I-945) and in accordance with the form instructions and applicable fees prescribed in 8 CFR 103.7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS will notify the alien of the bond amount, conditions, and the type of bond to submit. Failure to respond to USCIS’s solicitation for a bond or submission that does not comply with required amount/conditions will result in denial of the adjustment application. DHS plans separate operational guidance describing specifics of bond submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligor notification/change-of-address requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An obligor must notify DHS within 30 days of any change in the obligor’s or the alien’s physical and mailing address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contractual change-of-address requirement is similar to a sponsor’s obligation under 8 CFR 213a.3; additionally, the alien must comply with change-of-address requirements under section 265 of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1305, and 8 CFR 265.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond maintenance duration and cancellation triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: A public charge bond must remain in effect until the alien naturalizes/obtains U.S. citizenship, permanently departs the United States, dies, the bond is substituted with another bond, or the bond is otherwise cancelled by DHS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a condition of the bond, an alien agrees not to receive public benefits (as defined in 8 CFR 212.21(b)) after adjustment to LPR and until the bond is cancelled under proposed 8 CFR 213.1(g). Bonds may also be cancelled under statutory reasons or DHS determination of no likelihood of future public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and evidentiary standard for permanent departure
rubrics_metrics.description: Permanent departure for bond-cancellation purposes requires two elements: (1) the alien has lost or abandoned lawful permanent resident (LPR) status (voluntarily or involuntarily), and (2) the alien has physically left the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS proposes that involuntary loss of LPR status is only deemed in removal proceedings with a final order of removal or through rescission of adjustment of status. Abandonment of LPR status is fact-specific; courts look to length of absence, family and employment ties, property holdings, residence, and intent/actions. Aliens must provide evidence of official determination of loss of status before USCIS will cancel the bond when loss is by operation of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond substitution rules (limited-duration bonds)
rubrics_metrics.description: If USCIS accepts a bond of limited duration, a substitute bond must be submitted at least 180 days before the bond on file expires; substitute bonds may be submitted by the obligor, substitute obligor, or alien at any time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A substitute bond must be valid, properly submitted with appropriate fee, effective on the day the prior bond expires (or when the new bond takes effect if earlier), meet all requirements in 8 CFR 103.6 and 213.1, and cover any breach that occurred before USCIS accepted the substitute bond in case USCIS learns of the breach after expiration. If USCIS finds the substitute insufficient, it will notify the obligor to correct deficiencies within a stipulated timeframe; failure to correct results in rejection. Upon acceptance, the prior bond would be cancelled as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond breach definition (public benefits and other conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A bond is breached if the alien receives public benefits (as defined in proposed 8 CFR 212.21(b)) after adjustment to lawful permanent resident and until the bond is cancelled, or if the alien fails to comply with any other bond condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public benefits received while the alien is in a status exempt from the public charge ground, benefits received after naturalization, and certain military-related benefits (10 U.S.C. 504(b)(1)(B) or 504(b)(2) for active duty/Ready Reserve service or received by spouse/child) are not counted toward breach. Receipt of public assistance ordinarily sufficed historically to warrant continuation of a bond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breach recovery/payment process (agency repayment requests)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the alien became a public charge by using public assistance and an agency requests repayment, the obligor must pay the actual expenses to INS within thirty days; if no payment is made, the obligor is required to pay the total amount due plus $200 to INS, and if still unpaid the amount is extracted from the bond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, upon receipt of a repayment request from the public agency, INS applied this timeline and penalty structure; in a breach, the bond is applied to satisfy the necessary amount and any remainder continues in effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: INS/USCIS monitoring and review practice (historical context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, INS monitored posted public charge bonds periodically and would review bonds every 5 years if no cancellation request was made, cancelling bonds after review if the alien had not and would not likely become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any interested party could request review and cancellation of a bond at any time; upon request INS would notify the alien and allow presentation of evidence that the bond was not breached. The Examinations Handbook and AFM provide procedural guidance (e.g., posting, cancellation, breaching).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of benefits counted for breach/cancellation
rubrics_metrics.description: Only public benefits as defined in proposed 8 CFR 212.21(b) are counted in breach/cancellation determinations; certain benefits and circumstances are excluded from consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excluded from breach/cancellation consideration: benefits received while in a status exempt from public-charge inadmissibility under 8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(4); benefits received after U.S. citizenship; and certain military-related benefits. DHS will not count benefits received by enlistees (or their spouse/child) under specified statutory authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational processing fees
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes processing fees for the initial submission of the Public Charge Bond (Form I-945) and for the Request for Cancellation of Public Charge Bond (Form I-356); both fees would be initially set at $25.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form I-945 filing should include the $25 processing fee; USCIS plans to establish a process to accept and process public charge bonds available on the effective date of the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that bond submissions comply with 8 CFR 103.6 and 213.1
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitute and initial bonds must meet all requirements applicable to bonds as required by 8 CFR 103.6 and proposed 8 CFR 213.1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes procedural and form requirements (e.g., acceptable surety standards, submission procedures, and documentation) and ensures bonds confer continuous indemnification of the United States until cancellation criteria are satisfied.
